what_its_for: Furosemide is a 'water pill' (diuretic) that helps your body get rid of extra salt and water through your urine. It is used to treat swelling (edema) caused by heart failure, liver disease, or kidney disease. It is also used to treat high blood pressure.
how_to_take: Take furosemide by mouth with or without food. If it upsets your stomach, try taking it with food or milk. Because this medicine makes you urinate more often, try to take it in the morning or early afternoon so it does not disturb your sleep at night. Swallow the tablet whole with a full glass of water. If you are taking the liquid form, use the measuring device that came with your medicine — do not use a regular kitchen spoon.
dosing: Take furosemide exactly as your doctor prescribed. Your dose depends on your condition and how well you respond to treatment. Do not take more or less than directed. Your doctor may start you on a low dose and adjust it over time. Common doses range from 20 mg to 80 mg once or twice daily, but your doctor will tell you the right amount for you.
missed_dose: If you miss a dose, take it as soon as you remember — but only if it is still several hours before your bedtime, so you are not waking up at night to urinate. If it is close to your next scheduled dose, skip the missed dose and continue with your regular schedule. Do NOT take two doses at the same time to make up for a missed one.
storage: Store furosemide tablets at room temperature, between 59°F and 86°F (15°C to 30°C). Keep it away from light, heat, and moisture. Do not store it in the bathroom. Keep the liquid form in the refrigerator if directed on the label, and throw away any unused liquid after 60 to 90 days (check your bottle label). Keep all medicines out of reach of children and pets.
what_to_avoid: Avoid standing up too quickly from a sitting or lying position, as furosemide can cause dizziness or lightheadedness — this is more common when you first start the medicine. Avoid drinking large amounts of alcohol, as it can worsen dizziness and low blood pressure. Be careful in hot weather or during heavy exercise, as you can become dehydrated more easily. Avoid taking ibuprofen (Advil, Motrin), naproxen (Aleve), or other anti-inflammatory pain relievers unless your doctor approves, as they can reduce how well furosemide works and may harm your kidneys.
when_to_call_doctor: Call your doctor right away if you experience: severe dizziness or fainting, muscle cramps or weakness, unusual tiredness, dry mouth or extreme thirst, nausea or vomiting, decreased urination, hearing loss or ringing in the ears, signs of allergic reaction (rash, itching, swelling of face/lips/tongue, trouble breathing), or skin that blisters or peels. Also call your doctor if your swelling is getting worse or you gain more than 2 to 3 pounds in a day or 5 pounds in a week.
when_it_works: Furosemide works fairly quickly. If you take it by mouth, you will usually start urinating more within 30 to 60 minutes. The effect typically lasts about 6 to 8 hours. You may notice less swelling within a few days of starting treatment. For high blood pressure, it may take a few weeks to see the full benefit. Keep taking your medicine even if you feel well.
special_populations: Older adults: You may be more sensitive to the effects of furosemide, including dizziness and dehydration. Rise slowly from sitting or lying down to reduce your fall risk. Pregnant women: Talk to your doctor before using this medicine during pregnancy. It is generally not recommended unless clearly needed. Breastfeeding: Furosemide may pass into breast milk. Talk to your doctor before breastfeeding while taking this medicine. Kidney or liver disease: Your doctor will monitor you closely and may adjust your dose. Children: Furosemide can be used in children, but the dose is based on weight and will be determined by your child's doctor. Diabetes: Furosemide may affect your blood sugar levels. Monitor your blood sugar more closely and report any changes to your doctor.
